title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The community detection problem (1/2)

Nodes are people; an edge is a connection (messages, friendship, collaboration).
Goal: find groups of nodes that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the graph.
These groups may be groups of friends, or people who share interests.
Once the communities are found, we may:


Look for influencers and send them advertisements, or approach them directly.
Understand the common features of the nodes inside this community to understand how the community was created and what share the people inside of it.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The community detection problem (2/2)









Idea: density, not just connectivity


A community is not a connected component. It is a set of nodes with a higher density of internal edges than of edges leaving the set.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
What is a graph?




Definition (graph)


A graph is a pair \((V,E)\): \(V\) is the set of nodes, and \(E\subset V\times V\) is the set of edges.
A weighted graph is a triple \((V,E,W)\) with \(W\in\R^{|V|\times|V|}\). The entries of \(W\) are the weights.





Undirected graph: \((i,j)\in E\) implies \((j,i)\in E\).
Undirected weighted graph: the graph is undirected and \(W=W^\top\).
Four classical types: directed or not, weighted or not.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Four types of graphs





Undirected/directed and unweighted/weighted graphs.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: Complete graphs and a ring graph
text:
Complete graphs and a ring graph







Complete graphs \(K_4\), \(K_5\) and \(K_6\).










A directed ring graph.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Adjacency matrix




Definition (adjacency matrix)


Let \(G=(V,E)\). The adjacency matrix \(A\in\{0,1\}^{|V|\times|V|}\) is \[A_{ij}=1\quad\text{if }(i,j)\in E,\qquad A_{ij}=0\quad\text{otherwise.}\] For a weighted graph, \(A_{ij}=W_{ij}\) when \((i,j)\in E\) and \(A_{ij}=0\) otherwise.





If \(G\) is undirected, then \(A\) is symmetric.
Community detection is about the connectivity of \(G\), which is encoded in \(A\).
Everything is inside \(A\) (all graphs problems are matrix problems): Adjacency matrix is the central mathematical object in graph theory.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Connectivity and connected components




Definition (connected graph)


\(G=(V,E)\) is connected if a path of edges links all the nodes. A connected component is a connected subgraph with no edge to its complement. A connected partition is a partition of \(V\) into connected components.





Weighted version: the edges of the path must have nonzero weight. Unweighted graphs correspond to \(W=(1)_{i,j}\).





Remark


A nontrivial connected partition is an ideal setting: the communities do not interact. Rare in practice, but a good guide for algorithms.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Definition of the Laplacian




Definition (Laplacian)


Let \(A\) be the adjacency matrix of \(G\). The Laplacian is \[L=D-A,\qquad D={\rm diag}(d),\qquad d_i=\sum_{j\in V}A_{ij}\] where \(d_i\) is the degree of node \(i\).





Other definitions exist; we use this one throughout.
If \(G\) is undirected, then \(L\) is symmetric: the spectral theorem applies, and \(L=PDP^\top\) with \(P\) orthogonal.
The spectrum of \(L\) is the key object of spectral community detection.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Quadratic form and first properties




Proposition


Let \(G=(V,E,W)\) be undirected with \(W_{ij}\geq 0\). Then:

\(f^\top Lf=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2\) for every \(f\in\R^{|V|}\);
\(L\) is symmetric positive semidefinite;
\(0\) is an eigenvalue and \(L\mathbf{1}=0\).





Proof.


\(f^\top(D-A)f=\sum_i d_if_i^2-\sum_{(i,j)\in E}f_iW_{ij}f_j=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2\).
The right-hand side is \(\geq 0\), so \(L\succeq 0\).
\((L\mathbf{1})_i=d_i-\sum_j A_{ij}=0\). \(\square\)

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Multiplicity of \(0\) and connected components




Proposition


For an undirected weighted graph with nonnegative weights, the multiplicity of the eigenvalue \(0\) of \(L\) equals the number of connected components.
Moreover \({\rm Ker}(L)\) is spanned by \(\mathbf{1}_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{V_k}\), where \(V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) is the partition of \(V\) into connected components.








Idea: the kernel of \(L\) sees the communities


In the ideal case, the indicators of the communities are eigenvectors for \(\lambda=0\). Spectral methods start from this fact.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Proof sketch: one connected component
Assume \(G\) is connected and \(Lf=0\). Then \(f^\top Lf=0\), so \[\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2=0.\]


Weights are nonnegative, so \(W_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2=0\) on every edge: \(W_{ij}=0\) or \(f_i=f_j\).
Connectivity: any \(i,j\) are joined by a path of positive weights, so \(f\) is constant along the path.
Hence \(f\) is constant: \({\rm Ker}(L)={\rm span}(\mathbf{1})\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Proof sketch: several components
Up to reordering the nodes, \[L=\begin{pmatrix}L_1&&\\&\ddots&\\&&L_k\end{pmatrix},\] where \(L_i\) is the Laplacian of the \(i\)-th connected component.


Each \(L_i\) has kernel spanned by the constant vector on \(V_i\), so \(\mathbf{1}_{V_i}\in{\rm Ker}(L)\).
Conversely \(Lf=0\) if and only if \(L_if=0\) on each block, so \(f\) is constant on each \(V_i\).
Therefore \({\rm Ker}(L)={\rm span}(\mathbf{1}_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{V_k})\).





Remark


The same statement holds for unweighted undirected graphs, by taking \(W=(1)_{i,j}\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Example: the complete graph \(K_n\)
The Laplacian of \(K_n\) is \[L=nI_n-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top=\begin{pmatrix}n-1&-1&\cdots&-1\\-1&n-1&\cdots&-1\\\vdots&&\ddots&\vdots\\-1&-1&\cdots&n-1\end{pmatrix}.\]

If \(Lf=0\), then \(nf=\inr{f,\mathbf{1}}\mathbf{1}\), so \(f\in{\rm span}(\mathbf{1})\).
The multiplicity of \(0\) is \(1\), as expected: \(K_n\) is connected.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: Why is \(L\) called a Laplacian? Newton’s law of cooling
text:
Why is \(L\) called a Laplacian? Newton’s law of cooling


Imagine temperatures \(T_i\) on the nodes. Heat flows in proportion to the temperature difference: \[\frac{dT_i}{dt}=-\kappa\sum_{j\in V}A_{ij}(T_i-T_j).\]

Node \(i\) exchanges heat only with its neighbours.
In vector form: \(\dfrac{dT}{dt}=-\kappa(D-A)T=-\kappa LT\).
Compare with the heat equation \(\partial_t u=\alpha\Delta u\): one identifies \(L\) with \(-\Delta\).















Idea: a discrete Laplacian


The graph Laplacian is the discrete analog of the Laplacian of the heat equation.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Ideal setting: disjoint communities

Ideal case: the communities are the connected components. They do not interact.
Almost never true in practice (a few inter-community edges always exist), but a good guide.
Then \({\rm Ker}(L)={\rm span}(\mathbf{1}_{V_1},\ldots,\mathbf{1}_{V_k})\).
The indicators \(\mathbf{1}_{V_i}\) are hard to read off \(L\). An orthonormal basis \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\) of \({\rm Ker}(L)\) is easy.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: The spectral method in two steps
text:
The spectral method in two steps

Cluster the \(|V|\) row vectors \(y_i\in\R^k\) of the matrix \([u_1|\cdots|u_k]\) into \(k\) clusters \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\).
Return \(V_p=\{i\in V:y_i\in C_p\}\). These are the detected communities.






Idea: cluster the rows, not the nodes


Each node \(i\) is represented by the \(i\)-th row of the eigenbasis matrix. Clustering these rows clusters the nodes.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: Why the rotation does not destroy the clusters
text:
Why the rotation does not destroy the clusters

\(\{\mathbf{1}_{V_p}/\sqrt{|V_p|}\}_p\) is an orthonormal basis of \({\rm Ker}(L)\).
So is \(\{u_1,\ldots,u_k\}\): there is \(R\in{\rm O}(k)\) with \[[u_1|\cdots|u_k]=\big[\mathbf{1}_{V_1}/\sqrt{|V_1|}|\cdots|\mathbf{1}_{V_k}/\sqrt{|V_k|}\big]R.\]
The rows of the indicator matrix take only \(k\) distinct values. A \(k\)-means on these rows recovers the components exactly.
A rotation of \(\R^k\) preserves this clustering.


In practice \(G\) is not a disjoint union: look at the eigenspace of the \(k\) smallest eigenvalues, not only the kernel. Choose \(k\) by an elbow in the spectrum, or by a modularity function.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Graph cuts and modularity
Detecting communities \(\iff\) finding a partition that minimizes the inter-community weight while keeping the communities large enough.

A cut is a partition of \(V\).
A modularity quantifies intra- versus inter-community mass.

For \(A,B\subset V\), \[W(A,B)=\sum_{\substack{(i,j)\in E\\(i,j)\in A\times B}}(W_{ij}+W_{ji})=2\sum_{\substack{(i,j)\in E\\(i,j)\in A\times B}}W_{ij}.\]
The cut of a partition \(V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) is \[{\rm cut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k W(V_i,V_i^c).\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The mincut problem
For two communities, encode \(V_1\) by \(x\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}\): \[{\rm cut}(V_1,V_1^c)=2\sum_{(i,j)\in E}x_i W_{ij}(1-x_j).\]
\[\min_{x\in\{0,1\}^{|V|}}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}x_i W_{ij}(1-x_j).\]

Solvable by the Stoer–Wagner algorithm.
In practice it often returns a singleton: the node of smallest degree.






Remark


A singleton is not a community. One must force the parts to have sufficient size.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
RatioCut




Definition (RatioCut)


\[{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)=\frac12\sum_{i=1}^k\frac{W(V_i,V_i^c)}{|V_i|}.\]





The factor \(1/|V_i|\) penalizes small communities.
Minimizing RatioCut over \(\cP_k(V)\) is NP-hard in general.
We rewrite it as a vector (then matrix) problem and convexify the constraint. The relaxation is the spectral method.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Membership vector for two communities
For \(V_1\subset V\), set \[f_i^{V_1}=\begin{cases}\sqrt{|V_1^c|/|V_1|}& \text{if }i\in V_1,\\[4pt]-\sqrt{|V_1|/|V_1^c|}& \text{if }i\notin V_1.\end{cases}\]




Proposition


Let \(L\) be the Laplacian of an undirected weighted graph, and \(n=|V|\). Then

\(\inr{f^{V_1},\mathbf{1}}=0\) and \(\norm{f^{V_1}}_2^2=n\);
\((f^{V_1})^\top L f^{V_1}=n\,{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c)\).






So minimizing RatioCut \(\iff\) minimizing \(f^\top Lf\) over these discrete vectors \(f^{V_1}\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: Proof sketch of the RatioCut identity
text:
Proof sketch of the RatioCut identity
From the quadratic form, \[(f^{V_1})^\top Lf^{V_1}=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}W_{ij}(f_i^{V_1}-f_j^{V_1})^2.\]

The difference \(f_i^{V_1}-f_j^{V_1}\) is nonzero only across the cut.
On a cut edge, \[\Big(\sqrt{\tfrac{|V_1^c|}{|V_1|}}+\sqrt{\tfrac{|V_1|}{|V_1^c|}}\Big)^2=\frac{n}{|V_1|}+\frac{n}{|V_1^c|}.\]
Summing both orientations of the cut gives \(n\,{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c)\).
The two constraints: \(\norm{f^{V_1}}_2^2=|V_1|+|V_1^c|=n\) and \(\inr{f^{V_1},\mathbf{1}}=0\). \(\square\)

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Convex relaxation for \(k=2\)
Three equivalent discrete problems: \[\min_{V_1\subset V}(f^{V_1})^\top Lf^{V_1},\qquad\min_{V_1\subset V}\big((f^{V_1})^\top Lf^{V_1}:\norm{f^{V_1}}_2^2=n,\,\inr{f^{V_1},\mathbf{1}}=0\big),\] and \(\min_{V_1}{\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c)\). All are NP-hard.

The map \(f\mapsto f^\top Lf\) is convex (\({\rm Hess}=2L\succeq 0\)).
The difficulty is the discrete constraint \(f=f^{V_1}\).
Relax it to \(f\in\R^{|V|}\): \[\min_{f\in\R^{|V|}}\big(f^\top Lf:\norm{f}_2^2=1,\,\inr{f,\mathbf{1}}=0\big).\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The Fiedler vector




Definition (Fiedler vector)


A Fiedler vector of \(L\) is an eigenvector for the second smallest eigenvalue. That eigenvalue is the algebraic connectivity.








Proposition


The Fiedler vectors are exactly the solutions of the relaxed problem.




Proof. Write \(0=\lambda_1\leq\lambda_2\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\) and \(u_1=\mathbf{1}\). If \(\norm{f}_2=1\) and \(\inr{f,\mathbf{1}}=0\), \[f^\top Lf=\sum_{i=2}^n\lambda_i\inr{u_i,f}^2\geq\lambda_2,\] with equality at \(f=u_2\). \(\square\)

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: From a Fiedler vector to two communities
text:
From a Fiedler vector to two communities

A Fiedler vector \(u_2\) approximates the two-valued membership vector \(f^{V_1^*}\).
Its coordinates should concentrate around two values.
Cluster the coordinates of \(u_2\) into two classes \(C_1,C_2\) on \(\R\).
The communities are \(\{i:u_{2i}\in C_1\}\) and \(\{i:u_{2i}\in C_2\}\).


This is the spectral method for \(k=2\), with first eigenvector \(u_1=\mathbf{1}\) (clustering the rows of \([u_1|u_2]\) is the same as clustering the coordinates of \(u_2\)).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Membership matrix for \(k\) communities
To a partition \(V_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup V_k\) associate \(H\in\R^{|V|\times k}\) with columns \(h_j=\mathbf{1}_{V_j}/\sqrt{|V_j|}\): \[H_{ij}=\begin{cases}1/\sqrt{|V_j|}& \text{if }i\in V_j,\\0& \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}\]




Proposition


\(H^\top H=I_k\) and \({\rm RatioCut}(V_1,\ldots,V_k)={\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)\).





\(H^\top H=I_k\): the \(V_j\) are disjoint, and \(\sum_{i\in V_j}1/|V_j|=1\).
\({\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_p h_p^\top Lh_p=\sum_p W(V_p,V_p^c)/(2|V_p|)\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Relaxation for \(k\) communities
The discrete problems \(\min{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)\) over membership matrices \(H\) are NP-hard. The objective \(H\mapsto{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)\) is convex. Relax the combinatorial constraint: \[\min_{\substack{H\in\R^{|V|\times k}\\H^\top H=I_k}}{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH).\]
Write \(L=UDU^\top\) with \(0=\lambda_1\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_n\). Then \[{\rm Tr}(H^\top LH)=\sum_i\lambda_i\norm{a_i}_2^2,\qquad\sum_i\norm{a_i}_2^2=k,\] where \(a_i\) is the \(i\)-th row of \(U^\top H\). The minimum is \(\sum_{i=1}^k\lambda_i\), attained when \[{\rm span}(h_1,\ldots,h_k)={\rm span}(u_1,\ldots,u_k).\]

The solutions are orthonormal bases of the eigenspace of the \(k\) smallest eigenvalues.
Cluster the \(n\) rows of \(H\) into \(k\) groups: this is again the spectral method.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Algorithm of the spectral method




Algorithm (spectral method)


Input: Laplacian \(L\) of \(G\), and \(k\).

Compute an orthonormal basis of \(k\) eigenvectors for the \(k\) smallest eigenvalues of \(L\).
Form the \(n\times k\) matrix \(H\) with these columns.
Cluster the \(n\) rows \(y_1,\ldots,y_n\in\R^k\) into \(k\) clusters \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\).
Output: communities \(\{i:y_i\in C_p\}\), \(p=1,\ldots,k\).






Justified by the RatioCut relaxation, or by the ideal connected-component picture.
Choose \(k\) by an elbow in the spectrum of \(L\), or by evaluating a modularity (e.g. RatioCut) as a function of \(k\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Why a random graph?

Until now every edge was observed.
In applications (genes, companies, ) some links are missing or uncertain.
One then assumes a probabilistic model under the observations, and still wants the communities.
The same spectral method will be applied to the Laplacian of the observed adjacency matrix.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The Erdős–Rényi model




Definition (Erdős–Rényi)


\(G\sim G(n,p)\) is an undirected unweighted graph on \(n\) nodes with \[A_{ij}=A_{ji},\qquad A_{ii}=1,\qquad (A_{ij})_{j>i}\ \text{i.i.d. }{\rm Bern}(p).\]





Every pair of distinct nodes is connected independently with probability \(p\).
No community structure: a null model.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The stochastic block model




Definition (SBM)


\(G\sim G(n,p,q)\) with \(0\leq q<p\leq 1\) if there is a partition \(V=V_1\sqcup V_1^c\) such that, for \(i<j\), \[A_{ij}\sim\begin{cases}{\rm Bern}(p)&\text{if }i,j\text{ are in the same community},\\{\rm Bern}(q)&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\] and \(A_{ji}=A_{ij}\), \(A_{ii}=1\).





Intra-community edges are more likely than inter-community edges (\(p>q\)).
Problem: given one draw of \(G\), recover \(V_1\) and \(V_1^c\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Likelihood in the two-community SBM
Given \(A\), the likelihood at \((V_1,p,q)\) is \[\cL(V_1,p,q)=\prod_{(i,j)\in\cC}p^{A_{ij}}(1-p)^{1-A_{ij}}\prod_{(i,j)\in\cC^c}q^{A_{ij}}(1-q)^{1-A_{ij}},\] where \(\cC\) is the set of intra-community pairs \(i<j\) and \(\cC^c\) the inter-community pairs.

Write \(N_{\cC}=\sum_{(i,j)\in\cC}A_{ij}\) and \(P_{\cC}=N_{\cC}/|\cC|\) (and likewise for \(\cC^c\)).
The MLE maximizes \(\log\cL\) in \((V_1,p,q)\) under \(p\geq q\).
For equal-size communities, \(|\cC|=|\cC^c|=(n^2-n)/4\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Maximum likelihood equals RatioCut
For \(|V_1|=n/2\), maximizing in \((p,q)\) first (KKT) yields:

if \(P_{\cC}>P_{\cC^c}\), then \(\hat p=P_{\cC}\), \(\hat q=P_{\cC^c}\);
otherwise \(\hat p=\hat q=(P_{\cC}+P_{\cC^c})/2\), and the value does not depend on \(V_1\).

The remaining problem in \(V_1\) is to maximize an entropy under \(P_{\cC}\geq P_{\cC^c}\). Since \(P_{\cC}+P_{\cC^c}\) is constant, this is equivalent to minimizing \(P_{\cC^c}\).

\[P_{\cC^c}={\rm RatioCut}(V_1,V_1^c).\]




Idea: MLE is RatioCut


For two equal-size communities, the MLE in the SBM is the RatioCut problem.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
An equivalent discrete program




Remark


For \(|V_1|=n/2\) one has \(f^{V_1}\in\{-1,1\}^n\), so the MLE / RatioCut problem is \[\min\big(x^\top Lx:\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0,\,x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big).\] Since \(x^\top Lx=-x^\top Ax+\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}\) and the second term is constant, this is also \[\max\big(x^\top Ax:\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0,\,x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big).\]




This last form is the one we shall lift to an SDP.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Detectability: isolated nodes
If a node of \(V_1\) has no edge inside \(V_1\), there is no reason to assign it to \(V_1\). Exact recovery then fails.




Proposition


If \(p\leq\log(n/2)\,/\,(n/2-2)\), then \(\PP[\text{some node of }V_1\text{ is isolated in }V_1]\geq 1/2\).




Proof idea. Let \(A_i\) be the event that \(i\in V_1\) is isolated in \(V_1\), and \(N=|V_1|-1\). Then \(\PP[A_i]=(1-p)^N\). A Bonferroni bound \[\PP[\cup_i A_i]\geq(N+1)(1-p)^N-(N+1)N(1-p)^{2N-1}\] is at least \(1/2\) as soon as \(p\leq(\log N)/(N-1)\). \(\square\)

Exact recovery therefore requires \(p\gtrsim\alpha\log n\,/\,n\). The hard regime is \(q=\beta\log n\,/\,n\) with \(\beta<\alpha\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Information-theoretic phase transition




Theorem (phase transition in the equal-size SBM)


Let \(\hat V_1\) be the MLE (minimal RatioCut). If \(p=\alpha\log n\,/\,n\) and \(q=\beta\log n\,/\,n\), then:

if \(\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}>\sqrt{2}\), then \(\hat V_1,\hat V_1^c\) recover \(V_1,V_1^c\) with high probability;
if \(\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}<\sqrt{2}\), no algorithm succeeds with probability \(\geq 1/2\).






A sharp threshold, but the MLE is not computable.
The practical question: can a spectral or SDP method attain (or approach) this threshold?

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: Spectral method for the equal-size SBM
text:
Spectral method for the equal-size SBM




Lemma


If \(|V_1|=|V_1^c|=n/2\), the following are equivalent:

\(u_2\) is a Fiedler vector of \(\E L=\E(D-A)\);
\(u_2\) is a leading eigenvector of \[\E A-\Big[n\tfrac{p+q}{2}+(1-p)\Big]\Big(\tfrac{\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt n}\Big)\Big(\tfrac{\mathbf{1}}{\sqrt n}\Big)^\top.\]





Why. All mean degrees are equal, so \(\E D\) is a multiple of \(I_n\). Eigenvectors of \(\E L\) and \(\E A\) coincide (eigenvalues reversed). The leading eigenspace of \(\E A\) is \({\rm span}(\mathbf{1})\); removing it leaves the Fiedler direction.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
A practical spectral problem
We do not know \(\E A\), \(p\) or \(q\). Estimate:

\(\E A\) by \(A\);
\((p+q)/2\) by the edge density \[\lambda=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}A_{ij},\qquad \E\lambda=\frac{p+q}{2}-\frac{p-q}{n-1}.\]

The spectral method becomes \[\max_{\norm{x}_2\leq 1}\inr{x,(A-\lambda J_n)x},\qquad J_n=\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top.\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Matrix lifting
Under equal sizes, \(f^{V_1}\in\{-1,1\}^n\), and the discrete problem is \[\max_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}x^\top(A-\lambda J_n)x=\max_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}\inr{A-\lambda J_n,xx^\top}.\]
Passing from a quadratic function of \(x\) to a linear function of \(Z=xx^\top\) is matrix lifting.
The matrix \(Z=xx^\top\) satisfies: \(Z=Z^\top\), \(Z\succeq 0\), \({\rm diag}(Z)=I_n\), and \({\rm rank}(Z)=1\).





Idea: drop the rank


The only nonconvex constraint is \({\rm rank}(Z)=1\). Removing it yields an SDP.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
SDP relaxation
\[\max_{\substack{Z\succeq 0\\{\rm diag}(Z)\preceq I_n}}\inr{A-\lambda J_n,Z}.\]

If \(\hat Z\) is a solution, take a leading eigenvector \(\hat x\) and its sign.
\(\{i:{\rm sign}(\hat x_i)=1\}\) and its complement are the estimated communities.





Proposition


The oracle problem \(\max\inr{\E A-\alpha u_1\otimes u_1,Z}\) (same constraints) has the unique solution \(\bar x\otimes\bar x\), where \(\bar x_i=\pm 1\) is the true membership vector and \(\alpha=n(p+q)/2+(1-p)\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Algorithm of the SDP method




Algorithm (SDP relaxation)


Input: adjacency matrix \(A\) of a two-community equal-size SBM.

Compute \(\lambda=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}A_{ij}\).
Solve the SDP \(\max\inr{A-\lambda J_n,Z}\) over \(Z\succeq 0\), \({\rm diag}(Z)\preceq I_n\).
Take a leading eigenvector \(\hat x\) of the solution \(\hat Z\).
Output: \(\hat V_1=\{i:{\rm sign}(\hat x_i)=1\}\) and \(\hat V_1^c\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
What we want to prove
Observe \(A\sim{\rm SBM}(n,p,q)\) with equal-size communities. Let \(\hat Z\) be the SDP solution and \(\hat x\) a leading eigenvector. We want \(\hat x\) close to the membership \(\bar x\in\{\pm 1\}^n\).




Theorem (estimation of \(\bar x\bar x^\top\))


Assume \(n\geq 10^4\eps\), \(\max(p(1-p),q(1-q))\geq 20/n\), \(p\geq a/n\), \(q\geq b/n\) and \((a-b)^2\geq 10^4\eps^{-2}(a+b)\). Then, with probability at least \(1-e^3 5^{-n}\), \[\norm{\hat Z-\bar x\bar x^\top}_2^2\leq \eps n^2=\eps\norm{\bar x\bar x^\top}_2^2.\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
From matrices to vectors: Davis–Kahan




Corollary


Under the same assumptions, if \(\norm{\hat x}_2=\sqrt n\), then \[\min_{\alpha\in\{\pm 1\}}\norm{\alpha\hat x-\bar x}_2^2\leq 8\eps n=8\eps\norm{\bar x}_2^2.\]








Theorem (Davis–Kahan)


If \(A,B\) are symmetric and \(\lambda_i(A)\) has gap \(\delta>0\) from the rest of the spectrum, then \[\min_{\alpha\in\{\pm 1\}}\norm{u_i(A)-\alpha u_i(B)}_2\leq 2^{3/2}\frac{\norm{A-B}_2}{\delta}.\]




Apply it to \(A=\bar x\bar x^\top\) (gap \(\delta=n\)) and \(B=\hat Z\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Outline of the proof
Write \(\cM_{\rm opt}=\{Z:Z\succeq 0,\,{\rm diag}(Z)\preceq I_n\}\). Three steps:

Oracle: \(\bar Z=\bar x\bar x^\top\) maximizes \(Z\mapsto\inr{\E(A-\lambda J_n),Z}\) over \(\cM_{\rm opt}\) (as in the oracle proposition).
Uniform concentration: with high probability, \[\sup_{Z\in\cM_{\rm opt}}\big|\inr{(A-\lambda J_n)-\E(A-\lambda J_n),Z}\big|\] is small. This is the probabilistic step.
Curvature at the optimum: \(\inr{\E(A-\lambda J_n),\bar Z-Z}\gtrsim\norm{Z-\bar Z}_1\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Grothendieck’s inequality




Theorem (Grothendieck)


If \(\big|\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}s_it_j\big|\leq 1\) for all \(s_i,t_j\in\{\pm 1\}\), then for every Hilbert space \(H\) and unit vectors \(u_i,v_j\), \(\big|\sum_{i,j}b_{ij}\inr{u_i,v_j}\big|\leq K_G\), with \(K_G\leq 1.783\).




Write \(\cM_1=\{st^\top:s,t\in\{\pm 1\}^n\}\) and \(\cM_G=\{XY^\top:\text{rows of }X,Y\text{ in }B_2^n\}\).




Corollary


\(\displaystyle\sup_{Z\in\cM_G}\inr{B,Z}\leq K_G\sup_{Z\in\cM_1}\inr{B,Z}=K_G\norm{B}_{\infty\to 1}\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Why Grothendieck applies here




Proposition


\(\cM_{\rm opt}\subset\cM_G\).




If \(Z\succeq 0\) then \(Z=XX^\top\), and \({\rm diag}(Z)\preceq I_n\) means \(\norm{X_{i\bullet}}_2\leq 1\).

Therefore \[\sup_{Z\in\cM_{\rm opt}}\big|\inr{(A-\lambda J_n)-\E(\cdots),Z}\big|\leq K_G\norm{A-\E A}_{\infty\to 1}+K_G|\lambda-\E\lambda|\,\norm{J_n}_{\infty\to 1}.\]

Bound \(\norm{A-\E A}_{\infty\to 1}\) and \(|\lambda-\E\lambda|\) by Bernstein and a union bound.
If \(\bar p=\frac{2}{n(n-1)}\sum_{i<j}{\rm Var}(A_{ij})>9/n\), then with probability \(1-e^3 5^{-n}\), \[\norm{A-\E A}_{\infty\to 1}\leq 6n(n-1)\sqrt{\bar p/n}.\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Weak duality for SDP problems
A standard SDP and its dual: \[\min\big(\inr{C,X}:X\succeq 0,\,\cA(X)=b\big),\qquad\max\big(\inr{\lambda,b}:C-\cA^\top(\lambda)\succeq 0\big).\]

Weak duality: \(\inr{C,X}\geq\inr{\lambda,b}\) for every feasible pair.
If a feasible pair saturates the inequality, both are optimal: this is a dual certificate.





Theorem (strong duality for SDP)


If there exist \(X_0\succ 0\) with \(\cA(X_0)=b\) and \(\lambda_0\) with \(C-\cA^\top(\lambda_0)\succ 0\) (Slater), then both problems attain their optima and there is no duality gap.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The dual-certificate method




Proposition


If \(X^*\) is primal-feasible, \(\lambda^*\) is dual-feasible, and \(\inr{C,X^*}=\inr{b,\lambda^*}\), then both are optimal.




Strategy.

Start from an NP-hard problem \((P_0)\) (here, recover \(g=f^{V_1}\)).
Convexify it into an SDP \((P)\).
Take the candidate \(X_0=gg^\top\) and build a dual-feasible \(\lambda_0\) with equal objective values.
Then \(X_0\) solves \((P)\): one has solved \((P_0)\) by solving \((P)\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
section: Another SDP, designed for exact recovery
text:
Another SDP, designed for exact recovery
The theoretical problem with \(\E L\) has unique solutions \(f^{V_1}\) and \(f^{V_1^c}\). We observe only \(L\), so we solve the empirical version \[\max\big(x^\top Ax:\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0,\,x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big).\]

Dropping \(\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0\) makes \(\mathbf{1}\) optimal: the trivial cut.
Penalize: replace the objective by \(x^\top Ax-\lambda\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}^2\), and add the constant \(\lambda\norm{x}_2^2\).
For \(\lambda=1/2\) this is \(x^\top Bx\) with \[B=2A-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top-I_n,\qquad B_{ij}=\begin{cases}0&i=j,\\1&(i,j)\in E,\\-1&(i,j)\notin E.\end{cases}\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Lifted SDP
\[\max\big(x^\top Bx:x\in\{-1,1\}^n\big)\quad\rightsquigarrow\quad\max\big(\inr{B,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big).\]

The rank constraint has been dropped: this is an SDP.
From a solution \(\hat Z\): take a leading eigenvector and its sign, or round \(G\sim\cN(0,\hat Z)\) and take \({\rm sign}(G)\).
Goal: prove that \(gg^\top\) is the unique solution, by a strict dual certificate.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Dual of the community-detection SDP
The dual can be written \[\min\big({\rm Tr}(Y):Y-B\succeq 0,\,Y\text{ diagonal}\big).\]
Weak duality: for primal-feasible \(Z\) and dual-feasible \(Y\), \[\inr{B,Z}\leq{\rm Tr}(Y).\]
\(Y\) certifies a feasible \(Z\) when \(\inr{B,Z}={\rm Tr}(Y)\), i.e. \(\inr{B-Y,Z}=0\).

For uniqueness one needs a strict certificate: \({\rm Ker}(B-Y)\) of dimension \(1\).




Lemma


If \(Y\) certifies \(gg^\top\) and \(\dim{\rm Ker}(B-Y)=1\), then \(gg^\top\) is the unique primal solution.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Construction of the certificate
Conditions on \(Y\): diagonal, \(Y\succeq B\), \((B-Y)g=0\), and \(\lambda_2(Y-B)>0\).
The first three force \[Y_{ii}=\frac{(Bg)_i}{g_i}=\frac{2(Ag)_i}{g_i}-1,\qquad Y_{ij}=0\text{ for }i\neq j.\]




Proposition


If \(\lambda_2(Y-B)>0\), then \(gg^\top\) is the unique solution of the SDP.




It remains to prove \(\lambda_2(Y-B)>0\) with high probability in the SBM.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Deterministic plus concentration
Write \(\square=(\alpha-\beta)\log n\) when \(p=\alpha\log n\,/\,n\) and \(q=\beta\log n\,/\,n\). Enough to show:

\(\lambda_2(\E(Y-B))=\square\);
\(\norm{(Y-B)-\E(Y-B)}_{\rm op}<\square\) with high probability.

Weyl / Courant–Fischer then gives \[\lambda_2(Y-B)\geq\lambda_2(\E(Y-B))-\norm{(Y-B)-\E(Y-B)}_{\rm op}>0.\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Spectrum of the mean certificate
A computation with \(g\in\{\pm 1\}^n\) and \(\inr{g,\mathbf{1}}=0\) yields \[\E(Y-B)=n(p-q)I_n-(p-q)gg^\top+(1-p-q)\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top.\]

\(g\) is an eigenvector for the eigenvalue \(0\).
On \(g^\perp\), if \(p+q\leq 1\) then \(v^\top\E(Y-B)v\geq n(p-q)\), with equality for \(v\perp\mathbf{1}\).
Hence \(\lambda_2(\E(Y-B))=n(p-q)=(\alpha-\beta)\log n\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Decomposing intra- and inter-community edges








Figure 1: Adjacency matrix \(A=A^{\sim}+A^{\not\sim}\): intra-community blocks (blue) and inter-community blocks (red).






\(Y-B=2\big[(D^{\sim}-A^{\sim})-(D^{\not\sim}-A^{\not\sim})\big]+\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^\top\): difference of the two Laplacians.
Each Laplacian is a sum of independent matrices \(\Delta_{ij}=E_{ii}+E_{jj}-E_{ij}-E_{ji}\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Matrix Bernstein




Theorem (matrix Bernstein)


Let \(X_k\) be independent centered symmetric \(d\times d\) matrices with \(\lambda_{\max}(X_k)\leq R\) a.s. Then, with probability at least \(1-d\exp(-t)\), \[\lambda_{\max}\Big(\frac1n\sum_k X_k\Big)\leq\sigma\sqrt{\frac{2t}{n}}+\frac{2Rt}{3n},\qquad\sigma^2=\Big\|\frac1n\sum_k\E X_k^2\Big\|_{\rm op}.\]





The dimension \(d\) appears in the probability. Here \(t\sim\log n\), so it only costs constants.
Applied to the sum over intra- and inter-edges: \(R=2\) and \(\sigma^2\leq n(p+q)\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Exact recovery by SDP




Theorem


Let \(p=\alpha\log n\,/\,n\), \(q=\beta\log n\,/\,n\) with \(0<\beta<\alpha\) and \(p+q<1\), and \(|V_1|=n/2\). Then \[\{gg^\top\}=\argmax\big(\inr{B,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big)\] with probability at least \(1-2/n^\eps\), as soon as \[\sqrt{2(1+\eps)(\alpha+\beta)}+\frac{4(1+\eps)}{3}<\alpha-\beta.\]





An NP-hard problem is solved, for most SBM graphs, by an SDP.
The threshold is more restrictive than \(\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}>\sqrt{2}\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
No computational gap




Theorem (improved analysis)


Under the same SBM assumptions, \(gg^\top\) is the unique SDP solution with high probability as soon as \[\sqrt{\alpha}-\sqrt{\beta}>\sqrt{2}.\]







The SDP attains the information-theoretic threshold.
There is no computational gap for two equal-size communities in the SBM.






Idea: randomness does things well


NP-hard problems can become easy under a natural random model. Convex relaxation — of the objective, of the constraint, or by matrix lifting — is the right device.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Dual certificate for basis pursuit
The same idea applies to \[\min\big(\norm{t}_1:At=y\big).\]

Subdifferential: \(0\in\partial^-\norm{\cdot}_1(x^*)+\mathrm{Im}(A^\top)\) iff there is \(\beta^*\) with \[\norm{A^\top\beta^*}_\infty\leq 1,\qquad (A^\top\beta^*)_I={\rm sgn}(x^*_I),\quad I={\rm supp}(x^*).\]
Lagrangian dual: \(\max\big(\inr{\beta,y}:\norm{A^\top\beta}_\infty\leq 1\big)\).
Weak duality: \(\norm{t}_1\geq\inr{\beta,y}\). Equality plus dual feasibility certifies \(t^*\).

A strict certificate rules out every other feasible \(t\): that is uniqueness.




Proposition


Under strong duality, if \(\lambda^*\) solves the dual then \(x^*\) solves the primal if and only if \(\varphi(x^*)=\psi(\lambda^*)\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The lifting device

In compressed sensing and matrix completion one convexified the objective (\(\ell_0\), rank).
Here one convexifies a combinatorial constraint, after rewriting a quadratic \(x\mapsto x^\top Mx\) as the linear map \(Z\mapsto\inr{M,Z}\) on \(Z=xx^\top\).
Dropping \({\rm rank}(Z)=1\) is the SDP relaxation.
Two further examples: a leading eigenvector, and MAX-CUT.

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Lifting a leading eigenvector
\[u_1\in\argmax_{\norm{x}_2=1}\norm{Ax}_2\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\max_{\substack{Z\succeq 0\\{\rm rank}(Z)=1\\{\rm Tr}(Z)=1}}\inr{A^2,Z}.\]

\(\norm{Ax}_2^2=\inr{A^2,xx^\top}\) and \(\norm{x}_2=1\iff{\rm Tr}(xx^\top)=1\).
Drop the rank: \(\max\{\inr{A^2,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,{\rm Tr}(Z)=1\}\).






Remark


This relaxation is exact: \(\inr{A^2,Z}\leq\lambda_1(A)^2\), with equality at \(u_1u_1^\top\). If \(\lambda_1\) is simple, the SDP has the unique solution \(u_1u_1^\top\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The MAX-CUT problem
A cut is a partition \(S\sqcup S^c=V\). MAX-CUT maximizes the number of edges across the cut: \[\max_{S\subset V}\sum_{(i,j)\in E}\mathbf{1}_{i\in S,\,j\in S^c}=\max_{x\in\{\pm 1\}^n}\frac12\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(1-x_ix_j).\]
Equivalent form: \[\min\big(x^\top Ax:x_i^2=1\big).\]

The constraints \(x_i^2=1\) make the problem combinatorial.
Lift: \(x^\top Ax=\inr{A,xx^\top}\) and \(x_i^2=1\iff Z_{ii}=1\).

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
The Goemans–Williamson relaxation
\[\min\big(\inr{A,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1\big).\]
Rounding: draw \(G\sim\cN(0,Z_1)\) and set \(\hat u={\rm sign}(G)\). Then \[\E\Big[\frac12\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(1-\hat u_i\hat u_j)\Big]\geq 0.868\cdot{\rm OPT}.\]

The same Gaussian rounding appears in the proof of Grothendieck’s inequality.





Idea: bidual = SDP


A first Lagrangian dual of MAX-CUT, then a second dual of that dual, is the Goemans–Williamson SDP: \[\max_u\big(\inr{\mathbf{1},u}:A-{\rm Diag}(u)\succeq 0\big)\leq\min_{Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{ii}=1}\inr{A,Z}\leq\min_{x_i^2=1}x^\top Ax.\]

title: Spectral methods and SDP relaxations for community detection
text:
Lifting linear and quadratic constraints
The constraint \(\inr{x,\mathbf{1}}=0\) is linear in \(x\), hence not a linear function of \(xx^\top\). One can still lift it by adding one coordinate: \[\begin{pmatrix}1\\x\end{pmatrix}\rightsquigarrow Z=\begin{pmatrix}1&x^\top\\x&xx^\top\end{pmatrix}.\]
The equal-size community problem becomes the SDP \[\min\big(\inr{L,Z}:Z\succeq 0,\,Z_{00}=1,\,Z_{ii}=1,\,\inr{Z,A}=0\big),\] after dropping the rank. Linear terms live in the first row and column of \(Z\).





Idea: one extra dimension


Quadratic terms live in \(xx^\top\). Linear terms appear as soon as one lifts \((1,x)\) instead of \(x\).

The compressed sensing problem



Linear measurements \(y_i=\inr{x,X_i}\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), i.e. \[y=Ax,\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}X_1^\top\\ \vdots\\ X_m^\top\end{pmatrix}\in\R^{m\times N}\]
High-dimensional regime: \(m<N\) (often \(m\ll N\)).
Highly underdetermined system: infinitely many solutions.







Solving \(y=Ax\) with far more unknowns than equations.












Highly underdetermined system of linear equations


Given \(A\) and \(y\) find signal \(x\) such that \(Ax=y\). There are \(m\) equations and \(N\) unknown variables with \(N>>m\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Sparse vectors




Definition (sparsity)


\({\rm supp}(x)=\{j: x_j\neq0\}\) and \(\norm{x}_0=|{\rm supp}(x)|\). The vector \(x\) is \(s\)-sparse when \(\norm{x}_0\leq s\) and the set of all \(s\)-sparse vectors is \[\Sigma_s=\{x\in\R^N:\norm{x}_0\leq s\}.\]





Structured sparsity: \(x=F\theta\) with \(\theta\in\Sigma_s\) for a dictionary \(F\). Replace \(A\) by \(AF\).
Good dictionaries (e.g. wavelets) come from approximation theory.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The two CS problems










CS problem 1 — measurement design


Construct, in minimal number, measurement vectors \(X_1,\ldots,X_m\) such that every \(x\in\Sigma_s\) can be reconstructed efficiently from \(y=Ax\) and \(A\).














CS problem 2 — reconstruction algorithm


Given \(A\), construct an efficiently implementable map \(\Delta:\R^m\to\R^N\) such that \[\Delta(A, y=Ax)=x\qquad\text{for all }x\in\Sigma_s.\]






Uniformity: the same \(A\) must work for all \(s\)-sparse signals.
The “true” dimension of \(x\in\Sigma_s\) is \(s\): ideally \(m\sim s\), plus a price for not knowing the support.
Extension to noisy measurements \(y=Ax+\xi\) and approximatively sparse signals (see the LASSO in linear regression).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The \(\ell_0\) minimization procedure

The solution set of \(At=y\) is the affine space \(x+\kerA\) of dimension \(\geq N-m\), \(\kerA=\{t\in\R^N:At=0\}\).
Idea: The target signal is sparse, hence, pick the sparsest element of this space.
Def.: \(\norm{t}_0= |\{j\in[N]: t_j\neq0\}|\) is the size of the support of \(t\in\mathbb{R}^N\)





Definition (\(\ell_0\) minimization)


\[\hat x_0\in\argmin_{t\in\R^N:\,At=y}\norm{t}_0\tag{$P_0$}\]







Hope: \(\kerA\) is “well positioned”, so that \(x+\kerA\) meets \(\Sigma_s\) only at \(x\).
Geometrically: \(\kerA\) should be far from sparse vectors, close to “diagonal” directions.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
When is \(x\) the unique \(\ell_0\) solution?







Proposition


Let \(x\in\R^N\) with \(s=\norm{x}_0\). The following are equivalent:

\(x\) is the unique solution of \((P_0)\), i.e. \(\hat x_0=x\);
\(\big(x+\kerA\big)\cap\Sigma_s=\{x\}\).





Proof idea. Both statements say that every \(t\neq x\) with \(At=Ax\) has \(\norm{t}_0>s\).










Warning


This Proposition concerns only a single vector \(x\). CS asks for properties of \(A\) that work uniformly over all \(x\in\Sigma_s\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(m\geq 2s\) necessary measurements







Proposition


The following are equivalent:

for all \(x\neq z\in\Sigma_s\), \(Ax\neq Az\) (necessary for exact reconstruction over \(\Sigma_s\));
\(\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}=\{0\}\);
every \(m\times 2s\) submatrix of \(A\) is injective (hence \(m\geq 2s\)).










Key steps.

\(\Sigma_s-\Sigma_s=\Sigma_{2s}\), which gives 1 \(\Leftrightarrow\) 2.
A \(2s\)-sparse \(x\) supported on \(J\) gives \(Ax=A_{\cdot J}x_J\), which gives 2 \(\Leftrightarrow\) 3.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Uniform reconstruction of \(\ell_0\) minimization over \(\Sigma_s\)







Proposition


\(\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}=\{0\}\) \(\iff\) \(\displaystyle\argmin_{At=Ax}\norm{t}_0=\{x\}\) for all \(x\in\Sigma_s\).







Key steps.

(\(\Rightarrow\)) If \(At=Ax\) and \(t\neq x\), then \(x-t\in\kerA\) has \(\norm{x-t}_0>2s\), so \(\norm{t}_0>s\geq\norm{x}_0\).
(\(\Leftarrow\)) Let \(t\in\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}\) and write \(t=x-z\) with \(\norm{x}_0=\norm{z}_0\leq s\). Then \(z\) is solution of \(\displaystyle\min_{At=Ax}\norm{t}_0\) and so \(z=x\).





Exact reconstruction of all \(s\)-sparse vectors via \(\ell_0\)-minimization requires at least \(2s\) measurements. Can we find \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}\) with \(m=2s\) satisfying \(\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}=\{0\}\)?

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(m = 2s\) measurements suffice








Proposition (Vandermonde matrices)


For every \(N\geq 2s\) there is \(A\in\R^{\red{2}\red{s}\times N}\) with \(\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}=\{0\}\): \[A=\begin{pmatrix}1&\cdots&1\\ t_1&\cdots&t_N\\ \vdots&&\vdots\\ t_1^{2s-1}&\cdots&t_N^{2s-1}\end{pmatrix},\quad 0<t_1<\cdots<t_N.\]





Proof: Every \(2s\times2s\) minor is a Vandermonde determinant \(\prod_{k<l}(t_{j_l}-t_{j_k})\neq0\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Conclusion





\(m=2s\) is a necessary and sufficient number of measurements for the reconstruction of any \(s\)-sparse signal
Any \((2s)\times N\) Vandermonde matrix can be used as a measurement matrix
\(\ell_0\) minimization is a procedure that reconstruct any \(s\)-sparse signal given \(2s\) (Vandermonde) measurements.












Question


Can we compute the solution of a \(\ell_0\)-minimization problem?

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Procedures vs. algorithms

Procedure: a statistic, i.e. a measurable function of the data. No computational content.
Algorithm: a concrete routine implementing a procedure.



Brute-force algorithm for \((P_0)\):
For \(s = 1, 2, \ldots, N\) do
  For each \(J \subset [N]\) with \(|J| = s\) do
   Try to solve \(A_{\cdot J} x_J = y\)
   If solvable, stop at the first solution and return it.




Number of systems to solve: \(\sum_{j\leq s}\binom{N}{j}\sim (N/s)^s\), which is exponential in \(s\).
Example \(N=1000\), \(s=10\): \(\binom{N}{s}\geq10^{20}\) linear systems to solve. At \(10^{-10}\) second each, that is about 300 years.




Is there a faster algorithm to solve our \(\ell_0\)-minimization problems?

\(NP\): a candidate solution can be certified in polynomial time (e.g. \(k\)-clique).

Examples: traveling salesman, max clique, knapsack, graph coloring.







Classes of problems in decision theory.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(\ell_0\) minimization is NP-hard


Idea: we believe that \(\ell_0\)-minimization is a difficult optimization problem (i.e. NP-hard) because it searches the support \(S\subset\{1, \cdots,N\}\) of the signal – it is ‘combinatorial in nature’.
Strategy: reduce, in polynomial time, an \(NP\)-complete problem to the \((P_0)\) problem.












Theorem


The \(\ell_0\) minimization procedure \((P_0)\) is \(NP\)-hard in general.







Our baseline \(NP\)-complete problem : Partition by 3-element sets: given subsets \(\cC_1,\ldots,\cC_N\) of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|\cC_j|=3\), is there a sub-collection forming a partition of \(\{1,\ldots,m\}\)? (Ex. with \(m=6\) and \(N=5\))

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Proof: reduction from partitioning by 3-element sets
text:
Proof: reduction from partitioning by 3-element sets
Given a ‘partitioning by 3-element sets’ problem, we necessarily have \(3N\geq m\) and \(m\) is a multiple of \(3\) (otherwise there is no partition).


Encode. Columns \(a_j=\mathbb{1}_{\cC_j}\in\R^m\), \(A=[a_1|\cdots|a_N]\), \(y=(1,\ldots,1)^\top\). This takes polynomial time, since \(N\leq\binom m3\).




Lower bound. Each \(a_j\) has 3 nonzeros, so \(Ax=y\) implies \(\norm{x}_0\geq m/3\).




If \(\norm{\hat x_0}_0=m/3\): the \(m/3\) sets \(\{\cC_j: j\in{\rm supp}(\hat x_0)\}\) cover all \(m\) coordinates, hence are disjoint, hence form a partition.




If \(\norm{\hat x_0}_0>m/3\): no partition exists, since the indicator vector \(z\) of such a partition would satisfy \(Az=y\) with \(\norm{z}_0=m/3\).



As a consequence, if we could solve any \(\ell_0\)-minimization problem then we could solve the ‘Partition by 3-element sets’ problem. However, this problem is NP-complete, in particular, it is NP-hard and so we could solve any NP problem. Hence, the \(\ell_0\)-minimization problem is NP-hard.






Conclusion: \(\ell_0\) minimization is optimal in theory (\(m=2s\)) but unusable in practice.







“In general” matters: for the first \(2s\) Fourier coefficients, Prony’s algorithm solves \((P_0)\) in linear time, but it is neither robust nor stable (a 1795 algorithm used in DVD players). We will see other example of measurement matrices for which an efficient algorithm can be used to solve \((P_0)\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Convex relaxation: the convex envelope

The objective \(\norm{\cdot}_0\) is not convex, which is the root of the difficulty.
Idea: replace the \(\norm{\cdot}_0\) function by the ‘closest’ convex function below it.








Definition (convex envelope)


Let \(f:C\to\R\) on a convex set \(C\subset\R^N\). The convex envelope of \(f\) over \(C\) is the largest convex function \(g\) with \(g\leq f\) on \(C\). It is denoted by \({\rm conv}(f)\).








Well defined: a supremum of convex functions is convex.
On all of \(\R^N\), the envelope of \(\ell_0\) is \(0\), which is uninformative. So we restrict \(C\) to a ball.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Convex envelope












Exercise: What is the convex envelope over \([-1, 1]\) of the \(\ell_0\) function over \(\mathbb{R}\)?
What is the convex envelope over \([-1, 1]^N\) of the \(\ell_0\) function (over \(\mathbb{R}^N\))?

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(\ell_1\) is the convex envelope of \(\ell_0\)







Theorem


The \(\ell_1\) norm is the convex envelope of the \(\ell_0\) function on \(B_\infty^N\).





Proof sketch on \(B_1^N\). Let \(F={\rm conv}(\ell_0)\).


\(\norm{x}_1\leq\norm{x}_0\) on \(B_1^N\) and \(\ell_1\) is convex, so \(\norm{\cdot}_1\leq F\).




Squeeze: \(F(\pm e_i)=1\) and \(F(0)=0\).




Write \(x=\sum_j|x_j|\,{\rm sign}(x_j)e_j+(1-\norm{x}_1)\,0\) and use convexity: \[F(x)\leq\sum_j|x_j|F({\rm sign}(x_j)e_j)+(1-\norm{x}_1)F(0)=\norm{x}_1.\]

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Convex envelope of the \(\ell_0\) function










Convex relaxation= Replace the (non-convex) objective \(\ell_0\) function in \((P_0)\) by its convex envelope to get a convex optimization problem.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The Basis Pursuit procedure




Definition (Basis Pursuit)


\[\hat x\in\argmin_{t\in\R^N:\,At=y}\norm{t}_1\tag{BP}\]





(BP) is the convex relaxation of \((P_0)\).
\(\ell_1\) methods are everywhere: geophysics, radio astronomy, spectroscopy, medical imaging, LASSO, Dantzig selector, Matching Pursuit.











Take-away


Convex relaxation turns combinatorial searches into problems solvable with convex optimization. It is a reflex worth having.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Basis Pursuit as a linear program
text:
Basis Pursuit as a linear program


\[\min_{(z^{(+)},z^{(-)})\in\R^{2N}}\ \sum_{j=1}^N z_j^{(+)}+z_j^{(-)}\] \[\text{s.t. } [A\,|\,-A]\begin{bmatrix}z^{(+)}\\ z^{(-)}\end{bmatrix}=y,\quad \begin{bmatrix}z^{(+)}\\ z^{(-)}\end{bmatrix}\geq0\tag{LP}\]


Linear objective,
linear constraints.
LP problem in \(\bR^{2N}\)












Proposition: (BP) and (LP) are equivalent


\(\hat x\in\bR^N\mapsto(\hat x^+,\hat x^-)\in\bR^{2N}\) and \((\widehat{z^+},\widehat{z^-})\in\bR^{2N}\mapsto\widehat{z^+}-\widehat{z^-}\in\bR^N\) map solutions to solutions.
Where for all \(x\in\bR^N\), \(x^+=(x_j^+)_{j=1}^N\) and \(x^-=(x_j^-)_{j=1}^N\) with \(x^\pm_j=\max(0,\pm x_j)\).





Key inequalities:

for all \(t\in\bR\), \(t=t^+-t^-\) and \(|t| = t^+ + t^-\).
\(\norm{z^{(+)}-z^{(-)}}_{1}\leq\sum_j z_j^{(+)}+z_j^{(-)}\), with equality for \((x^+,x^-)\).


From a \(NP\)-hard problem to a linear program: the algorithmic complexity gain is big!
\(\Rightarrow\) What are the prices to pay?

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Exact reconstruction property \(RE(s)\)




Definition (\(RE(s)\))


A measurement matrix \(A\in\R^{m\times N}\) satisfies the exact reconstruction property of order \(s\) when, for every \(x\in\Sigma_s\), \[\argmin_{t\in\R^N}\big(\norm{t}_1:At=Ax\big)=\{x\}.\]








\(RE(s)\) characterizes the matrices for which Basis Pursuit solves the CS problem on \(\Sigma_s\).
First question: how many measurements does \(RE(s)\) require?
Second question: how can we construct \(A\) satisfying \(RE(s)\) with the minimal number \(m\) of rows?

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Lower bound on the number of measurements for exact reconstruction over \(\Sigma_s\) of Basis Pursuit
text:
Lower bound on the number of measurements for exact reconstruction over \(\Sigma_s\) of Basis Pursuit







Proposition


If \(A\in\R^{m\times N}\) satisfies \(RE(2s)\), then necessarily the number of measurements must satisfy \[
m\geq\frac{1}{\log5}\Big\lfloor\frac s2\Big\rfloor\log\Big(\Big\lfloor\frac{N}{8es}\Big\rfloor\Big)\ \gtrsim\ s\log\Big(\frac{eN}{s}\Big).
\]





Proof sketch.

Quotient map \(Q:\ell_1^N\to\ell_1^N/\kerA\), with \(\norm{Qx}_1=\min_{h\in\kerA}\norm{x+h}_1\) and \(\dim\leq m\).




\(RE(2s)\) makes \(Q\) an isometry on \(\Sigma_s\): \(\norm{Qx-Qy}_1=\norm{x-y}_1\).




Varshamov–Gilbert gives many well-separated points \(x(S)=s^{-1}\sum_{i\in S}e_i\) in the unit ball.




Volumetric argument: at most \(5^m\) such points in an \(m\)-dimensional ball. Compare.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Proof tools: Varshamov–Gilbert and volumetric arguments
text:
Proof tools: Varshamov–Gilbert and volumetric arguments










Lemma (Varshamov–Gilbert)


For \(s\leq N/2\) there is a family \(\cS\) of \(s\)-subsets of \([N]\) with \(|S_1\cap S_2|\leq\lfloor s/2\rfloor\) for \(S_1\neq S_2\), and \[\log|\cS|\geq\Big\lfloor\frac s2\Big\rfloor\log\Big(\Big\lfloor\frac{N}{8es}\Big\rfloor\Big).\]














Lemma (volumetric argument)


If \(B\) is the unit ball of a norm on \(\R^n\) and \(\Lambda\subset B\) is \(\eps\)-separated (w.r.t. \(B\)), then \(|\Lambda|\leq(1+2/\eps)^n\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: A first identified price for convex relaxation
text:
A first identified price for convex relaxation










Conclusion


Basis Pursuit needs \(m\gtrsim s\log(eN/s)\) measurements, versus \(2s\) measurements for \(\ell_0\). The huge computational gain costs only a logarithmic factor on the number necessary measurements.









Can we construct matrices satisfying \(RE(2s)\) with \(m\sim s\log(eN/s)\)?
Are they much more difficult to construct than, for instance, Vandermonde matrices?

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: From \(RE(s)\) to conditions that can be checked
text:
From \(RE(s)\) to conditions that can be checked

Part 1 introduced ‘Basis Pursuit’: \(\hat x\in\argmin_{At=y}\norm{t}_1\) is a linear program (huge algorithmic gain compare with a NP-hard algorithm)
Part 2 showed that \(RE(s)\) forces \(m\gtrsim s\log(eN/s)\).


Goal of Part 3: conditions on \(A\) that imply \(RE(s)\), and matrices that satisfy them with the optimal number of measurements \(m\sim s\log(eN/s).\)









Roadmap


\[RIP(65s)\ \Longrightarrow\ Gelfand(s)\ \Longrightarrow\ NSP(s)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ RE(s)\]
Gaussian matrices satisfy RIP(\(s\)) with high probability when \(m\sim s \log(eN/s)\).





Randomness comes into the game!

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The Null Space Property \(NSP(s)\)







Idea



For \(\ell_0\): we needed \(\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}=\{0\}\).
For \(\ell_1\): \(\kerA\) must be far from sparse vectors.









Definition (\(NSP(s)\))


We say that \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}\) satisfies the Null Space Property of order \(s\) when, for every \(|J|=s\) and every \(v\in\kerA\setminus\{0\}\), \[\norm{v_J}_1<\norm{v_{J^c}}_1.\]
Notation: \(v_J\) coincides with \(v\) on \(J\) and is zero outside \(J\).





Equivalently, \(v_1^*+\cdots+v_s^*<\norm{v}_1/2\): no \(s\) coordinates carry half of the \(\ell_1\) mass. Kernel vectors are well spread.





\(NSP(s)\Rightarrow\kerA\cap\Sigma_{2s}=\{0\}\), and even “almost sparse” vectors are excluded from \(\kerA\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(NSP(s)\) is equivalent to exact reconstruction




Theorem



\(A\) satisfies \(RE(s)\) \(\iff\) \(A\) satisfies \(NSP(s)\).






\(RE\Rightarrow NSP\). For \(v\in\kerA\setminus\{0\}\) and \(|J|=s\), take \(x=-v_J\in\Sigma_s\). Then \[\norm{v_J}_1=\norm{x}_1<\norm{x+v}_1=\norm{v_{J^c}}_1.\]


\(NSP\Rightarrow RE\). For \(x\in\Sigma_s\) with \({\rm supp}(x)\subset J\) and \(v\in\kerA\setminus\{0\}\): \[\norm{x+v}_1=\norm{v_{J^c}}_1+\norm{x+v_J}_1\geq\norm{x}_1+\norm{v_{J^c}}_1-\norm{v_J}_1>\norm{x}_1.\]






\(NSP\) is necessary and sufficient, but we do not know how to check it directly on a given matrix. We need an easier way to characterize this property.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Geometric picture of \(NSP\)



\(\frac{1}{\sqrt N}B_2^N\subset B_1^N\subset B_2^N\), so \({\rm diam}(B_1^N,\ell_2^N)=1\).
The diameter is attained on the canonical axes, the sparsest vectors.
\(\kerA\) should avoid them and follow diagonal directions, where \(\norm{v}_2\ll\norm{v}_1\).
So \(B_1^N\cap\kerA\) should have a small Euclidean diameter.
















If \({\rm diam}(B_1^N\cap{\rm Ker}(A),\ell_2^N)\) is small enough, then \(NSP(s)\) should be true.





Remark: \(B_1^N\) is the unit ball of the \(\ell_1^N\) norm in \(\bR^N\), it is therefore a convex set. However, the representation of \(B_1^N\) above highlights the fact that \(B_1^N\) is mostly the \(\frac{1}{\sqrt N}B_2^N\) ball with picks at \(\pm e_j\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The Gelfand property




Definition (\(Gelfand(s)\))


\(A\) satisfies the Gelfand property of order \(s\) when \[{\rm diam}\big(B_1^N\cap\kerA,\ \ell_2^N\big)<\frac{1}{2\sqrt s}.\]





\(\dim\kerA\geq N-m\) is huge, yet its section of \(B_1^N\) must have diameter \(\ll1\).
Connected to Euclidean sections of \(B_1^N\) in the asymptotic theory of Banach spaces.











Key Idea in CS


The Gelfand property is a very restrictive condition: we don’t know (so far) how to construct in a deterministic way matrices having this property for the optimal number \(m\sim s \log(eN/s)\). However, we will show that random matrices nevertheless satisfy it.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(Gelfand(s) \Rightarrow NSP(s)\)




Theorem



If \(A\) satisfies \(Gelfand(s)\), then \(A\) satisfies \(NSP(s)\).







Proof.

For \(v\in\kerA\setminus\{0\}\), \(v/\norm{v}_1\in B_1^N\cap\kerA\), hence \(\norm{v}_2<\norm{v}_1/(2\sqrt s)\).
For \(|J|=s\), Cauchy–Schwarz on \(s\) coordinates gives \[\norm{v_J}_1\leq\sqrt s\norm{v_J}_2\leq\sqrt s\norm{v}_2<\frac{\norm{v}_1}{2}.\]





Gelfand is still a property of the kernel. It is easier to study the action of \(A\) on sparse vectors directly. We therefore introduce now our last property: the RIP.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The Restricted Isometry Property \(RIP(s)\)




Definition (\(RIP(s)\))


\(A\in\R^{m\times N}\) satisfies the Restricted Isometry Property of order \(s\) when, for every \(x\in\Sigma_s\), \[\frac12\norm{x}_2\leq\frac{\norm{Ax}_2}{\sqrt m}\leq\frac32\norm{x}_2.\]






\(A\) cannot be an isometry on \(\R^N\) (huge kernel), only restricted to \(\Sigma_s\).
\(A\) is almost an isometry on \(\Sigma_s\), so \(\kerA\) stays away from sparse vectors.
Normalization matters: \(RE\), \(NSP\) and \(Gelfand\) only depend on \(\kerA\), but RIP depends on \(A\) itself. With \(\Gamma=A/\sqrt m\): \(\frac12\norm{x}_2\leq\norm{\Gamma x}_2\leq\frac32\norm{x}_2\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(RIP(s) \Rightarrow Gelfand(s/65)\)







Theorem


If \(A\) satisfies \(RIP(s)\), then \(A\) satisfies \(Gelfand(s/65)\). (Constant \(65\) is not optimal; \(s/2\) is possible.)









Proof sketch. Let \(v\in\kerA\setminus\{0\}\). Split its indices into blocks \(I_1,I_2,\ldots\) of size \(s\), sorted by decreasing \(|v_j|\).


Block comparison: \(\norm{v_{I_j}}_2\leq\sqrt s\norm{v_{I_j}}_\infty\leq\norm{v_{I_{j-1}}}_1/\sqrt s\).
First block, with \(Av=0\) and RIP: \[\norm{v_{I_1}}_2\leq\tfrac{2}{\sqrt m}\Big\|A\sum_{j\geq2}v_{I_j}\Big\|_2\leq3\sum_{j\geq2}\norm{v_{I_j}}_2\leq\tfrac{3}{\sqrt s}\norm{v}_1.\]
The tail gives \(\norm{\sum_{j\geq2}v_{I_j}}_2\leq\norm{v}_1/\sqrt s\), so \[\norm{v}_2\leq\tfrac{4}{\sqrt s}\norm{v}_1<\tfrac{1}{2\sqrt{s/65}}\norm{v}_1.\]








Decreasing rearrangement of \(|v_j|\), cut into blocks of size \(s\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The chain of implications







Conclusion


\[RIP(65s)\ \Longrightarrow\ Gelfand(s)\ \Longrightarrow\ NSP(s)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ RE(s)\] To reconstruct every \(s\)-sparse vector by Basis Pursuit, it suffices to build a matrix satisfying \(RIP(65s)\).






Can we construct \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times N}\) satisfying \(RIP(65s)\) with \(m\sim s \log(ep/s)\)?



The only known constructions of RIP matrices with \(m\sim s\log(eN/s)\) rows are random.
Deterministic constructions reach only \(m\sim s^2\). Reaching \(s\log(eN/s)\) deterministically is a major open problem (still unsolved by OpenAI even though they have results on ‘derandomization’).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Standard Gaussian random matrices




Definition


A standard Gaussian matrix \(G\in\R^{m\times N}\) has \(mN\) i.i.d. \(\cN(0,1)\) entries. Its rows are standard Gaussian vectors \(\cN_N(0,I_N)\).





Concentration: for \(g\sim\cN(\mu,\sigma^2)\), \(\bP\big[|g-\mu|\geq t\sigma\big]\leq2e^{-t^2/2}, \forall t>0\).
Not every variable concentrates: Cauchy variables have no mean for instance.
Exponential variables concentrate “like \(e^{-t}\)” only.



Deviation: only the tail \(t\mapsto\bP[|X|\geq t]\) for large \(t\) matters.

Sub-Gaussian (\(\psi_2\)): \(\bP[|X|\geq t]\leq2e^{-c_1t^2}\).
Sub-exponential (\(\psi_1\)): \(\bP[|X|\geq t]\leq2e^{-c_1t}\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential variables







Proposition (moments vs. tails)


For \(\alpha\geq1\), the following are equivalent:

\(\norm{X}_{L_p}\leq c_0\,p^{1/\alpha}\) for every \(p\geq\alpha\);
\(\bP[|X|\geq t]\leq\exp(-t^\alpha/c_2^\alpha)\) for every \(t\geq c_1\).






Sub-Gaussian: moments grow like \(\sqrt p\). Sub-exponential: moments grow like \(p\).
Proof idea: Markov with an optimized \(p=[t/(ec_0)]^\alpha\) gives one direction; bounding \(\E\exp\big((|X|/c)^\alpha\big)\leq e\) gives the other. (See the Proposition 3.3 in the lecture notes for a detailed proof).









Proposition


If \(X\) is sub-Gaussian, then \(X^2\) is sub-exponential: \(\norm{X^2}_{L_q}=\norm{X}_{L_{2q}}^2\leq2c_0^2q\).





Why it matters: \(\frac1m\norm{Ax}_2^2\) is an average of squares.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Bernstein’s inequality







Proposition (Bernstein, sub-exponential case)


Let \(Z_1,\ldots,Z_m\) be i.i.d. copies of \(Z\) with \(\norm{Z}_{L_p}\leq C_0p\) for all \(p\geq1\). Then for every \(t>0\), \[\bP\Big[\Big|\frac1m\sum_{i=1}^mZ_i-\E Z\Big|\geq tC_0\Big]\leq2\exp\big(-c_1m\min(t^2,t)\big)\] where \(c_1>0\) is some absolute constant.





A non-asymptotic CLT-type statement (with a Gaussian and exponential regimes), valid for every fixed \(m\).


Proof sketch (Laplace transform).

Chernoff bound: \(\bP[\bar Z_m\geq t]\leq\inf_{\lambda>0}e^{-\lambda t}\prod_i\E e^{\lambda Z_i/m}\).
Taylor expansion and \(k!\geq(k/e)^k\): \(\ \E e^{\mu Z}\leq\exp\big((e\mu C_0)^2/(1-e\mu C_0)\big)\).
Optimize \(\lambda\): a Gaussian regime \(e^{-cmt^2}\) for small \(t\), an exponential regime \(e^{-cmt}\) for large \(t\).

(See Proposition 3.5 in the lecture notes for a detailed proof)

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Gaussian matrices satisfy RIP







Theorem


Let \(G\in\R^{m\times N}\) be a standard Gaussian matrix. If \(m\geq c_1s\log(eN/s)\), then with probability at least \(1-2\exp(-c_0m)\), for every \(x\in\Sigma_s\), \[\frac12\norm{x}_2\leq\frac{\norm{Gx}_2}{\sqrt m}\leq\frac32\norm{x}_2.\]






More generally, \(\Gamma=\frac{1}{\sqrt m}A\), where the rows of \(A\) are i.i.d. copies of \(X\) that is

isotropic: \(\E\inr{X,x}^2=\norm{x}_2^2, \forall x\in\bR^N\);
sub-Gaussian: \(\norm{\inr{X,x}}_{L_p}\leq C_0\norm{x}_2\sqrt p, \forall x\in\bR^N, p\in\bN^*\).



Exo. 1: Show that \(X\sim\cN_N(0, I_N)\) is an isotropic and sub-Gaussian vector.
Exo. 2: Show that \(RIP(s)\) is implied by \(\sup_{x\in \Sigma_s\cap S_2^{N-1}}\big| \frac{\norm{Gx}_2^2}{m} - 1 \big|\leq \frac{1}{4}\), where \(S_2^{N-1}=\{x\in\bR^N: \norm{x}_2=1\}\).
Exo. 3: Show that \(\Sigma_s\cap S_2^{N-1} = \cup_{J:|J|=s} S_2^J\) where \(S_2^J = \{x\in\bR^N: \norm{x}_2=1, {\rm supp x}\subset J\}\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Proof tools: \(\varepsilon\)-nets and operator norm







Lemma (Size of an \(\varepsilon\)-net of \(S_2^{s-1}\))


For \(0<\eps<1\), there is \(\Lambda_\eps\subset S_2^{s-1}\) with \(|\Lambda_\eps|\leq(5/\eps)^s\) such that every \(x\in S_2^{s-1}\) is within \(\eps\) of \(\Lambda_\eps\).





Proof: take a maximal \(\eps\)-separated set. The disjoint balls \(x+\frac\eps2B_2^s\) fit inside \((1+\frac\eps2)B_2^s\); compare volumes.












Lemma


For \(B\in\R^{s\times s}\) symmetric, \(0<\eps<1/2\) and \(\Lambda_\eps\) an \(\eps\)-net of \(S_2^{s-1}\), we have \[\norm{B}_{op}=\sup_{x\in S_2^{s-1}}|\inr{Bx,x}|\leq(1-2\eps)^{-1}\max_{y\in\Lambda_\eps}|\inr{By,y}|\] where \(\norm{B}_{op}:= \sup_{\norm{x}_2=1}\norm{Bx}_2\).





Proof: diagonalize \(B\) for the first equality; then approximate \(x\in S_2^{s-1}\) by \(y\in\Lambda_\eps\) and show \(|\inr{Bx,x}|\leq |\inr{By,y}|+2\norm{x-y}_2\norm{B}\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Proof sketch: union bound over supports
text:
Proof sketch: union bound over supports
Goal: Prove that \(\displaystyle\sup_{x\in\Sigma_s\cap S_2^{N-1}}\big|\norm{\Gamma x}_2^2-1\big|\leq\frac14\) holds w.h.p. for \(\Gamma=A/\sqrt{m}\).



One point. \(\norm{\Gamma x}_2^2=\frac1m\sum_i\inr{X_i,x}^2\) is an average of sub-exponential variables with mean \(1\). Bernstein gives \(\big|\norm{\Gamma x}_2^2-1\big|\leq\frac18\) with probability \(\geq1-2e^{-c_0m}\).



Reduce to finitely many points. \(\Sigma_s\cap S_2^{N-1}=\bigcup_{|J|=s}S^J\). Apply the operator-norm lemma to \(B=\Gamma_J^\top\Gamma_J-I_s\) on each support: \[\sup_{x\in\Sigma_s\cap S_2^{N-1}}\big|\norm{\Gamma x}_2^2-1\big|\leq(1-2\eps)^{-1}\max_{x\in\Lambda_\eps}\big|\norm{\Gamma x}_2^2-1\big|.\]
Count. \(|\Lambda_\eps|\leq\binom Ns(5/\eps)^s\leq\big(5eN/(s\eps)\big)^s\).
Union bound. If \(\frac{c_0}{2}m\geq s\log\big(5eN/(s\eps)\big)\), all points of \(\Lambda_\eps\) succeed with probability \(\geq1-2e^{-c_0m/2}\). Take \(\eps=1/4\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Conclusion: \(m \sim s\log(eN/s)\) random measurements for BP are enough
text:
Conclusion: \(m \sim s\log(eN/s)\) random measurements for BP are enough


With high probability, Gaussian matrices satisfy \(RIP(s)\) with the optimal number of rows \(m\sim s\log(eN/s)\).
Taking \(m\sim s\log(eN/s)\) i.i.d. Gaussian measurement vectors, every \(s\)-sparse signal is recovered exactly by Basis Pursuit, i.e. by linear programming.









Procedure
Measurements needed
Computation




\(\ell_0\) minimization
\(m=2s\) deterministic
\(NP\)-hard


Basis Pursuit

linear program

section: Lab session on the phase transition diagram
text:
Lab session on the phase transition diagram


Open the notebook 0_lab_phase_transition_cvx.ipynb



Aim: Given a sparsity level \(s\), find the minimum number of measurements \(m\) needed to recover a signal \(x\) from its measurements \(y=Ax\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: The linear model with deterministic design
text:
The linear model with deterministic design

Input/output data \((X_i,Y_i)\), \(X_i\in\R^p\), \(Y_i\in\R\). Statistical modeling turns a real problem into a mathematical one.
Deterministic design (\(n\) noisy linear deterministic measurements with signals in \(\mathbb{R}^p\)): the \(X_i\in\mathbb{R}^p\) are fixed and \[
Y_i=\inr{X_i,\beta^*}+\varepsilon_i,\qquad\E\varepsilon_i=0,\quad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]

notation: \(m\to n\) number of measurements = number of data and \(N \to p\): dimensional of the signal \(\beta^*\). . . .

Matrix form: \(y=x\beta^*+\varepsilon\), with design matrix \(x\in\R^{n\times p}\) whose rows are \(X_i^\top\)
Normalization: \(x^\top x/n\) has ones on the diagonal, and the columns of \(x\) are centered.
Empirical risk: \(\ r(\beta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n(Y_i-\inr{X_i,\beta})^2\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Prediction risk and estimation risk

Prediction (denoising) risk: \[R(\beta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\big(\inr{X_i,\beta}-\inr{X_i,\beta^*}\big)^2=\frac1n\norm{x(\beta-\beta^*)}_2^2.\]
Estimation risk: \(\norm{\hat\beta-\beta^*}_q\) for some \(q\geq1\).
Results are stated with high probability or in expectation.









Other models


Random design (“statistical” model \(Y=\inr{X,\beta^*}+\varepsilon\), or learning theory with no model) uses the same estimators but harder tools: concentration and complexity. Here we stick to the deterministic design.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The least-squares estimator (OLS)




Definition (OLS)


\[\hat\beta_{OLS}\in\argmin_{\beta\in\R^p}\norm{y-x\beta}_2^2.\] It is unique iff \({\rm rank}(x)=p\), i.e. \(x^\top x\) is invertible, and then \[\hat\beta_{OLS}=(x^\top x)^{-1}x^\top y.\]





\(F(\beta)=\norm{y-x\beta}_2^2\) is convex, and \(\nabla F(\hat\beta)=-2x^\top(y-x\hat\beta)=0\).
\({\rm rank}(x)=p\) requires \(p\leq n\): more observations than parameters.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
OLS risk: \(p\sigma^2/n\)







Theorem


If the \(\varepsilon_i\) are independent, centered, with variance \(\sigma^2\), then \[\E\norm{x(\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta^*)}_2^2=p\sigma^2,\qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad\E\,R(\hat\beta_{OLS})=\frac{p\sigma^2}{n}.\]





Proof.

\(x(\hat\beta_{OLS}-\beta^*)=x(x^\top x)^{-1}x^\top\varepsilon=P\varepsilon\), with \(P\) the projection onto \({\rm Im}(x)\).
\(\norm{P\varepsilon}_2^2={\rm Tr}\big[(x^\top x)^{-1}x^\top\varepsilon\varepsilon^\top x\big]\).
Take expectations with \(\E\varepsilon\varepsilon^\top=\sigma^2I_n\): the result is \(\sigma^2{\rm Tr}(I_p)=p\sigma^2\).




Rate \(=\dfrac{(\#\text{parameters})\times(\text{noise variance})}{\#\text{observations}}\): each parameter costs \(\sigma^2/n\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
High-dimensional problems: \(p \gg n\)

OLS needs \(p\leq n\), and its risk grows linearly with \(p\).
Genomics example: \(n\approx30\) patients, \(p\approx30\,000\) genes.
Without extra assumptions, \(\beta^*\) cannot be estimated.









Sparsity assumption


Only a few genes are responsible for the disease: \(\beta^*\) is sparse, \(\ |{\rm supp}(\beta^*)|\leq n\ll p\), but its support is unknown.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Sparsity and the oracle that knows the support
text:
Sparsity and the oracle that knows the support

If an oracle revealed \(S^*={\rm supp}(\beta^*)\), we would run OLS on the coordinates in \(S^*\): \[\hat\beta^{(S^*)}=\argmin\big\{r(\beta):\beta_j=0\ \text{for } j\notin S^*\big\}.\]



The OLS theorem then gives \[\E\norm{x(\hat\beta^{(S^*)}-\beta^*)}_2^2=\sigma^2|S^*|\ \ll\ \sigma^2p.\]









Warning


\(S^*\) is unknown. The question is how much we pay for not knowing it.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(\ell_0\) penalization: AIC and BIC




Definition (\(\ell_0\)-penalized least squares)


\[\hat\beta_\lambda\in\argmin_{\beta\in\R^p}\Big\{\norm{y-x\beta}_2^2+\lambda\norm{\beta}_0\Big\}\] More generally, \(\hat\beta_f\in\argmin_\beta\big\{\norm{y-x\beta}_2^2+f(\norm{\beta}_0)\big\}\) with \(f\) increasing.





Penalize vectors that are not sparse enough.
AIC: \(\lambda=2\sigma^2\) (Akaike, after Mallows’ \(C_p\)).
BIC: \(\lambda=\sigma^2\log n\) (Schwarz).
Both require knowing \(\sigma^2\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Optimal rate for \(\ell_0\) penalization: \(s\log(ep/s)\)







Theorem [BTW07]


Deterministic design, \(\varepsilon_i\) i.i.d. \(\cN(0,\sigma^2)\). With \[f(k)=\frac{2\sigma^2k}{n}\Big(1+\tfrac{3}{\sqrt2}\sqrt{2\log\tfrac{ep}{k\vee1}}+4\log\tfrac{ep}{k\vee1}\Big),\] \[\E\norm{x(\hat\beta_f-\beta^*)}_2^2\leq5\norm{\beta^*}_0\,\sigma^2\Big(1+\log\frac{ep}{\norm{\beta^*}_0\vee1}\Big)+7\sigma^2.\]





The order \(\norm{\beta^*}_0\log(p/\norm{\beta^*}_0)\) is optimal, up to constants.
Compared with the oracle: the price for not knowing the support is only a \(\log(p/s)\) factor.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The implementation problem: \(2^p\) subsets

No known algorithm is really faster than exhaustive search: for each \(J\subset\{1,\ldots,p\}\), compute \(\hat\beta^{(J)}\) and compare \[\norm{y-x\hat\beta^{(J)}}_2^2+\lambda\norm{\hat\beta^{(J)}}_0.\]
This means \(2^p\) least-squares problems.



\(p=10\): fine. Genomics, \(p=30\,000\): \(2^{30000}>10^{9030}\) subsets.







Warning


The same obstruction as in Part 2: the \(\ell_0\) “norm” is optimal in theory, unusable in practice.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
The LASSO: \(\ell_1\) penalization




Definition (LASSO, Tibshirani 1996)


\[\tilde\beta_\lambda\in\argmin_{\beta\in\R^p}\Big\{\norm{y-x\beta}_2^2+\lambda\norm{\beta}_1\Big\},\qquad\lambda>0.\]





Replace \(\norm{\beta}_0\) by the convex \(\norm{\beta}_1\), giving a convex optimization problem.
Computable very fast, even for very large \(p\).
Theoretical guarantees close to those of \(\ell_0\) penalization, at the price of an assumption on the design \(x\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
\(\ell_1\) as the convex envelope of \(\ell_0\) (again)







Theorem


The \(\ell_1\) norm is the convex envelope of \(\ell_0\) on \(B_\infty^p\).





Same argument as in Part 2: \(\norm{\cdot}_1\leq{\rm conv}(\ell_0)\) by convexity, and the squeeze \(F(\pm e_i)=1\), \(F(0)=0\) gives the reverse inequality.




Compressed sensing (Part 2) \[\min_{At=y}\norm{t}_0\ \leadsto\ \min_{At=y}\norm{t}_1\]

Regression (Part 4) \[\norm{y-x\beta}_2^2+\lambda\norm{\beta}_0\ \leadsto\ \norm{y-x\beta}_2^2+\lambda\norm{\beta}_1\]

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Conditions on the design: RIP and compatibility \(\Phi(L,S)\)
text:
Conditions on the design: RIP and compatibility \(\Phi(L,S)\)

All conditions in the literature resemble RIP: \((1-\delta)\norm{\beta}_2\leq\norm{A\beta}_2\leq(1+\delta)\norm{\beta}_2\) for \(\beta\in\Sigma_s\).
Unlike CS, we estimate a single \(\beta^*\), so conditions may depend on \(S^*={\rm supp}(\beta^*)\) only.
The lower bound (a restricted smallest singular value) is the hard part.






Definition (compatibility constant)


For \(L>0\) and \(S\subset\{1,\ldots,p\}\), \[\Phi(L,S)=\min\Big\{\frac{|S|}{n}\norm{x\beta}_2^2:\ \norm{\beta_S}_1=1,\ \norm{\beta_{S^c}}_1\leq L\Big\}.\]





\(\Phi(L,S^*)>0\) asks \(x\) to be injective on a cone of vectors concentrated on \(S^*\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Oracle inequality under the compatibility condition
text:
Oracle inequality under the compatibility condition







Theorem


Let \(\Omega_0=\{2\norm{x^\top\varepsilon}_\infty\leq\lambda_0\}\), \(\lambda>\lambda_0\), \(L=\frac{\lambda+\lambda_0}{\lambda-\lambda_0}\), and assume \(\Phi(L,S^*)>0\). On \(\Omega_0\):

\(\displaystyle\norm{x\tilde\beta_\lambda-x\beta^*}_2^2\leq\frac{4\lambda^2|S^*|}{n\,\Phi(L,S^*)}\);
\(\displaystyle\norm{\tilde\beta_\lambda-\beta^*}_1\leq\frac{4\lambda^2|S^*|}{n(\lambda-\lambda_0)\Phi(L,S^*)}\).






Proof sketch.

Dual bound: \(|\inr{\varepsilon,x(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)}|\leq\norm{x^\top\varepsilon}_\infty\norm{\tilde\beta-\beta^*}_1\).
Basic inequality from the definition of \(\tilde\beta_\lambda\), split on \(S^*\) and \((S^*)^c\): \(\norm{x(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)}_2^2\leq2\lambda\norm{(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)_{S^*}}_1\) and \(\norm{\tilde\beta_{(S^*)^c}}_1\leq L\norm{(\tilde\beta-\beta^*)_{S^*}}_1\).
The error lies in the cone, so \(\Phi(L,S^*)\) turns the \(\ell_1\) bound into a prediction bound.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Controlling the noise: the event \(\Omega_0\)

We need \(2\norm{x^\top\varepsilon}_\infty\leq\lambda_0\) with high probability.



Chernoff and a union bound over the \(p\) columns \(C_j\) of \(x\): \[\bP\big[\norm{x^\top\varepsilon}_\infty\geq t\big]\leq e^{-\lambda t}\sum_{j=1}^p\E e^{\lambda\inr{C_j,\varepsilon}}.\]
Gaussian Laplace transform (\(\E e^{\mu g}=e^{\mu^2\sigma^2/2}\)) with \(\norm{C_j}_2^2=n\) gives \(\bP[\cdot]\leq p\,e^{-t^2/(2n\sigma^2)}\).
With probability \(\geq1-\eta\): \(\ \norm{x^\top\varepsilon}_\infty\leq\sigma\sqrt{2n\log(p/\eta)}\).










Consequence


Taking \(\lambda_0=2\sigma\sqrt{2n\log(p/\eta)}\) and \(\lambda=2\lambda_0\) (so \(L=3\)), with probability \(\geq1-\eta\), \[\norm{x(\tilde\beta_\lambda-\beta^*)}_2^2\leq\frac{128\,\sigma^2|S^*|\log(p/\eta)}{\Phi(3,S^*)}.\] This is the oracle rate \(\sigma^2|S^*|\), up to a \(\log p\) factor. Bounded noise also works (Hoeffding).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Oracle inequality under the restricted eigenvalue condition
text:
Oracle inequality under the restricted eigenvalue condition







Theorem ([Lasso3])


Deterministic design, \(\varepsilon_i\) i.i.d. \(\cN(0,\sigma^2)\). Assume that for some \(c>0\), \[\frac1c\leq\inf\Big\{\frac{v^\top(x^\top x/n)v}{\sum_{j\in J}v_j^2}:\ \sum_{j\notin J}|v_j|\leq3\sum_{j\in J}|v_j|,\ |J|\leq\norm{\beta^*}_0\Big\}.\] With \(\lambda=4\sigma\sqrt{2n\log(p/\eta)}\), with probability \(\geq1-\eta\), \[\norm{x(\tilde\beta_\lambda-\beta^*)}_2^2\leq128\,c\,\sigma^2\norm{\beta^*}_0\log\frac p\eta.\]





Without the cone constraint, this is the smallest eigenvalue of \(x^\top x/n\), which is \(0\) when \(p>n\).
Restricted to the cone \(\{\norm{v_{J^c}}_1\leq3\norm{v_J}_1\}\), it can stay positive.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Proof sketch for the LASSO bound
text:
Proof sketch for the LASSO bound

Noise event (lemma): \(\norm{x^\top\varepsilon}_\infty\leq\sigma\sqrt{2n\log(p/\eta)}=\lambda/4\) with probability \(\geq1-\eta\).



Basic inequality with \(v=\tilde\beta_\lambda-\beta^*\) and \(J={\rm supp}(\beta^*)\): \[\norm{xv}_2^2+\frac\lambda2\norm{v}_1\leq2\lambda\sum_{j\in J}|v_j|.\]




Cone: this gives \(\sum_{j\notin J}|v_j|\leq3\sum_{j\in J}|v_j|\), so the restricted eigenvalue condition applies: \[\sum_{j\in J}v_j^2\leq\frac cn\norm{xv}_2^2.\]




Close: Cauchy–Schwarz gives \(\norm{xv}_2^2\leq2\lambda\sqrt{\norm{\beta^*}_0\frac cn}\norm{xv}_2\), hence \(\norm{xv}_2^2\leq\frac{4\lambda^2c}{n}\norm{\beta^*}_0\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: Computing the LASSO: constrained form and duality
text:
Computing the LASSO: constrained form and duality

The penalized problem and the constrained problem \[\min_{b\in\R^p}\norm{y-xb}_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad\norm{b}_1\leq t\] have the same solution sets as \(\lambda\) ranges over \(\R_+\) and \(t\) over \(\R_+^*\).
Reason: a convex objective with a convex constraint under constraint qualification, so Lagrangian duality applies.


Forward stagewise heuristic: start at \(\beta(0)=0\). At each step, find the column most correlated with the residual, \[j(k)=\argmax_j|x_j^\top(y-x\beta(k))|,\] and move by a small step: \(\beta(k+1)=\beta(k)+\zeta\,{\rm sgn}(c_{j(k)})e_{j(k)}\).

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
section: The LARS algorithm and the regularization path
text:
The LARS algorithm and the regularization path

LARS (Efron, Hastie, Johnstone, Tibshirani): an exact, refined version that detects when a new variable enters.
Active set \(\cA(k)\), with \(\norm{\beta(k)}_0=k\) up to \(k=n\): \[\cA(k+1)=\cA(k)\cup\argmax_j|x_j^\top(y-x\beta(k))|.\]
Update along an equiangular direction: \(\beta(k+1)=\beta(k)+\gamma_{k+1}w_{k+1}\), where \(w_{k+1}\) solves \(x_{\cA}^\top x_{\cA}u=\mathbf 1\).








Proposition


The set of LASSO solutions, as \(t\) varies, is a piecewise linear path whose nodes are \(\beta(0),\beta(1),\ldots\)





In practice: lars(y, x) in R computes the whole path, and plot(lars(y, x)) draws the regularization path.

title: Compressed sensing, high-dimensional statistics and the \(\ell_1\) norm
text:
Link with compressed sensing


Noiseless regression = CS. We observe \(y=x\beta\) with \(p>n\), so the system has infinitely many solutions.

Sparsest solution: \(\beta^*=\argmin_b\{\norm{b}_0:y=xb\}\) is \(NP\)-hard.
Convex relaxation: \(\tilde\beta=\argmin_b\{\norm{b}_1:y=xb\}\) is LP.









Answer


Under design conditions very similar to the restricted eigenvalue condition (NSP, RIP), \(\tilde\beta=\beta^*\).





LASSO is the noisy version of Basis Pursuit: the same \(\ell_1\) relaxation, the same cone geometry, and the same RIP-type conditions.
